stem: What is the main function of the **testa** of a bean seed?

options.content: To store food for the embryo
options.rationale: Food is stored in the cotyledons.

options.content: To let water into the seed
options.rationale: Water enters mainly through the micropyle; the testa is a protective coat.

options.content: To protect the embryo from damage, microorganisms and drying out
options.rationale: The testa is the tough seed coat around the embryo and its food store.

options.content: To grow into the first root
options.rationale: The radicle grows into the first root.

explanation: The testa is the seed coat. It protects the embryo from physical damage, insects and microorganisms, and stops the seed from drying out.

stem: Which part of the embryo in a seed grows into the **root** of the seedling?

options.content: The radicle
options.rationale: The radicle is the young root; it is the first part to grow out of the seed.

options.content: The plumule
options.rationale: The plumule is the young shoot.

options.content: The cotyledon
options.rationale: Cotyledons store food (or absorb it from the endosperm in maize).

options.content: The hilum
options.rationale: The hilum is a scar on the testa, not part of the embryo.

explanation: The embryo has a radicle (young root), a plumule (young shoot) and one or two cotyledons. The radicle emerges first and grows down.

stem: Name the scar on the testa of a bean seed that shows where the seed was attached to the pod.

rejected.feedback: The micropyle is the tiny pore beside the scar. The scar itself is the hilum.
The testa is the whole seed coat. The scar on it is the hilum.
The plumule is the young shoot inside the seed. The scar is the hilum.

explanation: The hilum is the scar left where the seed was joined to the inside of the pod by a short stalk. The micropyle is the tiny pore next to it.
hints: It is a scar, not a pore.

stem: True or false: a maize grain is a fruit, not just a seed.

answerSpec.feedbackTrue: Correct: a maize grain is a one-seeded fruit. Its fruit wall is fused with the testa of the single seed inside.
answerSpec.feedbackFalse: It is true: a maize grain develops from a whole ovary. It is a one-seeded fruit whose fruit wall is fused with the testa.

explanation: Each maize grain forms from a whole ovary containing one ovule. The ovary wall becomes a thin fruit wall fused to the testa, so the grain is a one-seeded fruit.
hints: Did the grain form from an ovule or from a whole ovary?

stem: Combretum trees in msasa woodland produce dry fruits with four thin, papery wings. How are these fruits dispersed?

options.content: By animals that eat them
options.rationale: Animal-eaten fruits are fleshy and sweet; these are dry and papery.

options.content: By wind
options.rationale: Thin wings give a large surface area, so the fruit falls slowly and drifts on the wind.

options.content: By water
options.rationale: Water-dispersed fruits float because of air-filled tissue; wings are an adaptation to air.

options.content: By an explosive pod
options.rationale: Explosive fruits are pods that split and fling seeds; these fruits have wings instead.

explanation: The papery wings increase the surface area and air resistance of the fruit, so it falls slowly and is carried away by the wind.

stem: Match each fruit or seed with the way it is dispersed.

left.content: Mazhanje fruit with sweet, soft flesh
Msasa pod that dries and splits suddenly
Coconut with a fibrous, air-filled husk

right.content: Carried on the fur of animals or on clothing
Eaten by animals; the seeds pass out in droppings or are spat out
Thrown out by the plant itself
Carried to the stigma by insects

explanation: Barbs catch on fur and clothing; sweet flesh is eaten; drying pods split explosively; wings catch the wind; an air-filled husk floats. Insects carrying pollen to stigmas is pollination, not dispersal.
hints: Look for the feature in each description: barbs, flesh, splitting pod, wings, air-filled husk.

stem: Where is most of the food stored in a bean seed?

options.content: In the endosperm
options.rationale: The endosperm is the food store of a maize grain; a mature bean seed has none.

options.content: In the testa
options.rationale: The testa is a thin protective coat.

options.content: In the radicle
options.rationale: The radicle is the young root; it is tiny.

options.content: In the two cotyledons
options.rationale: The two large, fleshy cotyledons store starch and protein.

explanation: A bean is a dicotyledon: its two cotyledons are large and fleshy and store the food that the embryo uses during germination.

stem: A soaked sorghum grain is cut lengthwise and iodine solution is added to the cut surface. Which part turns **blue-black**?

options.content: The plumule
options.rationale: The young shoot contains very little starch.

options.content: The endosperm
options.rationale: The endosperm is the starch store of a cereal grain such as sorghum or maize, so iodine turns it blue-black.

options.content: The radicle
options.rationale: The young root contains very little starch.

options.content: The fruit wall
options.rationale: The thin fruit wall is mostly fibre, not starch.

explanation: Iodine solution turns blue-black with starch. A sorghum grain has the same plan as a maize grain: most of the starch is in the endosperm, and the embryo stays a paler colour.
hints: Which part of a cereal grain is the food store?

stem: Complete the description of a bean seed.

payload.template: The seed is covered by a tough {{blank:testa}}. Water enters through a tiny pore called the {{blank:micropyle}}. Inside, food is stored in two {{blank:cotyledons}}. The young shoot of the embryo is called the {{blank:plumule}}.

explanation: A bean seed has a testa outside, with a hilum (scar) and a micropyle (pore). Inside are two food-storing cotyledons and the embryo's radicle (root) and plumule (shoot).

stem: Marula fruits are eaten by elephants and other animals. Why is it an advantage for the tree that its seeds are enclosed in a very hard, thick stone?

options.content: The seed survives being swallowed and passes out undamaged in the animal's droppings
options.rationale: A hard covering protects the embryo from chewing and digestion, so it can germinate where it is deposited.

options.content: The heavy stone makes the fruit fall straight down under the parent tree
options.rationale: Falling under the parent is what dispersal avoids.

options.content: The stone attracts animals with its colour and scent
options.rationale: Animals are attracted by the sweet, scented flesh, not the stone.

options.content: The stone floats, so the seed is dispersed by water
options.rationale: Marula is dispersed by animals that eat its fruits.

explanation: Animals eat the sweet flesh and swallow or discard the stone. The hard covering protects the seed from teeth and digestive enzymes, so the seed is deposited alive, often far from the parent and with manure around it.
hints: What must happen to the seed inside an animal's gut?

stem: Select **all** the ways in which seed dispersal helps a plant species.

options.content: It reduces overcrowding and competition between the seedlings and the parent
options.rationale: Seedlings spread out compete less for light, water, mineral ions and space.

options.content: It makes sure that the seedlings grow in the shade of the parent
options.rationale: Shade from the parent reduces light for photosynthesis; dispersal moves seedlings away from it.

options.content: It allows the species to colonise new areas
options.rationale: Seeds that travel can establish the species in new places.

options.content: It makes sure that pollen reaches the stigma
options.rationale: That is pollination, not dispersal.

options.content: It improves the chance that some seedlings survive if conditions change in one place
options.rationale: Spreading seeds over many places spreads the risk.

options.content: It increases the number of seeds each plant makes
options.rationale: Dispersal moves seeds; it does not change how many are made.

explanation: Dispersal reduces overcrowding and competition, lets the species colonise new areas, and spreads its seedlings over many places so that more are likely to survive.
hints: Think about what would happen if every seed fell beneath its parent.

stem: Nyasha finds a small, hard structure on the ground. It has a scar at one end where it was attached to a plant, and another small scar at the opposite end. What is it most likely to be, and why?

options.content: A seed, because it has a hilum
options.rationale: A seed has only one scar, the hilum (with a micropyle beside it).

options.content: A seed, because it is hard
options.rationale: Many fruits and seeds are hard; hardness does not tell them apart.

options.content: A fruit, because it has two scars: one from its stalk and one from the style
options.rationale: Fruits develop from ovaries, which had both a stalk and a style.

options.content: A fruit, because it has a micropyle
options.rationale: The micropyle is a feature of seeds (it was the gap in the ovule).

explanation: A fruit develops from an ovary, which was attached by a stalk and carried a style, so it has two scars. A seed has only one scar, the hilum, beside its micropyle.
hints: Count the scars. What was attached to an ovary that was not attached to an ovule?

stem: Which statement correctly compares a bean seed with a maize grain?

options.content: Both store most of their food in an endosperm
options.rationale: Only maize does; a bean stores food in its cotyledons.

options.content: The bean has one cotyledon and the maize grain has two
options.rationale: It is the other way round: bean two, maize one.

options.content: The testa of the maize grain can be peeled off easily, but the bean's cannot
options.rationale: The maize testa is fused with the fruit wall; it is the bean's testa that peels off after soaking.

options.content: The bean stores food in two cotyledons; the maize grain stores food in its endosperm and has one cotyledon
options.rationale: This is the key difference between a dicotyledon and a monocotyledon seed.

explanation: A bean (dicotyledon) has two food-storing cotyledons and no endosperm. A maize grain (monocotyledon) has one cotyledon and stores food in a large endosperm; its testa is fused with the fruit wall.
hints: Dicotyledon means two seed leaves; monocotyledon means one.

stem: Name the part of the embryo that grows into the **shoot** of a seedling.

rejected.feedback: The radicle grows into the root. The young shoot is the plumule.
Cotyledons store or absorb food. The young shoot is the plumule.
The coleoptile is the sheath that protects the young shoot of maize; the shoot itself is the plumule.

explanation: The plumule is the young shoot of the embryo. It grows upwards, and its first leaves begin photosynthesis.
hints: The young root is the radicle; the young shoot has a different name.

stem: Jacaranda seeds are flat, with a thin papery wing around the edge. How does the wing help the seed to be dispersed?

options.content: It makes the seed lighter so that it is blown away
options.rationale: A wing adds a little mass; its job is to add surface area.

options.content: It increases the surface area and air resistance, so the seed falls slowly and drifts further in the wind
options.rationale: A slow fall gives the wind more time to carry the seed sideways.

options.content: It photosynthesises to give the seed energy during its flight
options.rationale: The wing is dry, dead tissue; it does not photosynthesise.

options.content: It attracts birds, which carry the seed away
options.rationale: Bird-dispersed fruits are fleshy and brightly coloured, not papery.

explanation: The wing gives a large surface area and air resistance. The seed falls slowly, so even a light breeze can carry it well away from the parent tree.
hints: Compare dropping a flat sheet of paper with the same sheet crumpled into a ball.

stem: On a farm near Masvingo, blackjack plants grow thickly along cattle paths and footpaths, even far from where the farmer first saw them. Which explanation is **best**?

options.content: Blackjack seeds are blown along the paths by the wind
options.rationale: Blackjack fruits have no wings or hairs; their barbed bristles suit animal dispersal.

options.content: Cattle eat the sweet blackjack fruits and pass out the seeds
options.rationale: Blackjack fruits are dry and thin, not fleshy and sweet.

options.content: The barbed fruits hook onto the hair of cattle and the clothes of people, and fall off along the paths
options.rationale: Animals and people moving along paths carry the hooked fruits and drop them there.

options.content: The pods explode and throw the seeds along the paths
options.rationale: Blackjack does not have explosive pods, and explosive pods throw seeds only a short distance.

explanation: Each blackjack fruit has barbed bristles that catch on fur and clothing. Cattle and people walking along the paths carry the fruits and drop them, so the weed spreads along the paths.
hints: Which animals use those paths, and what do blackjack fruits cling to?

stem:
Sipho investigated how the thin, papery wing of jacaranda seeds affects their fall. He dropped each seed from a height of $1.5\ \text{m}$ in a still room and timed its fall. He tested three seeds with the whole wing, three with half of the wing cut away and three with all of the wing cut away.

| Seeds | Fall times / s |
| --- | --- |
| Whole wing | 2.2, 2.4, 2.3 |
| Half of the wing removed | 1.4, 1.2, 1.3 |
| All of the wing removed | 0.6, 0.6, 0.6 |

parts.label: (a)
parts.stem: Calculate the mean fall time of the seeds with the whole wing.

parts.label: (b)
parts.stem: Which conclusion do the results support?

options.content: The wing makes no difference to how fast the seeds fall.
options.rationale: Mean fall times range from $0.6\ \text{s}$ to $2.3\ \text{s}$.

options.content: Seeds without a wing fall more slowly.
options.rationale: Seeds without a wing fell fastest.

options.content: The more wing area a seed has, the more slowly it falls.
options.rationale: Fall time fell from $2.3\ \text{s}$ to $1.3\ \text{s}$ to $0.6\ \text{s}$ as the wing was cut away.

options.content: The wing makes the seeds heavier, so they fall faster.
options.rationale: Seeds with a wing fell more slowly, not faster.

parts.label: (c)
parts.stem: Explain how a slower fall helps the tree to disperse its seeds.

points.description: The seed stays in the air for longer
So the wind can carry it further from the parent tree (less competition / overcrowding)

parts.explanation: A slowly falling seed stays in the air longer, so the wind carries it further from the parent tree, where its seedling will compete less with the parent.

parts.label: (d)
parts.stem: Suggest why Sipho tested three seeds of each type rather than one.

points.description: To make the results more reliable / so an unusual seed or a timing error has less effect on the mean

parts.explanation: Repeating with three seeds makes the results more reliable, because one unusual seed or one timing mistake has less effect on the mean.

parts.label: (e)
parts.stem: State **one** variable, other than the height, that Sipho should keep the same.

points.description: Any one: no draughts (still air) / seeds of similar size and mass (from the same tree) / the same person timing / the same way of releasing the seed

parts.explanation: For example, he should use seeds of a similar size from the same tree, or keep the air still for every drop.

explanation: The mean fall time with the whole wing is $(2.2 + 2.4 + 2.3) \div 3 = 2.3\ \text{s}$. Cutting the wing away shortened the fall, so the wing slows the fall; a slow fall lets the wind carry the seed further from the parent tree.
workedSolution:
**(a)** $(2.2 + 2.4 + 2.3) \div 3 = 6.9 \div 3 = 2.3\ \text{s}$.

**(b)** Less wing area → faster fall (2.3 s → 1.3 s → 0.6 s).

**(c)** Longer in the air → carried further by the wind → less competition with the parent.

**(d)** Reliability.

**(e)** Still air, similar seeds, same timer, same release method.
hints: Add the three times and divide by three.

stem:
Chipo investigated how water enters bean seeds. She used two groups of 10 bean seeds. In group A she sealed the micropyle of every seed with a tiny drop of nail varnish; group B was left untreated. She weighed each group, soaked the seeds in water for 6 hours, dried their surfaces and weighed them again.

| Group | Mass before soaking / g | Mass after soaking / g |
| --- | --- | --- |
| A: micropyles sealed | 5.20 | 6.24 |
| B: untreated | 5.00 | 7.90 |

parts.label: (a)
parts.stem: Calculate the percentage increase in mass of group B.

parts.label: (b)
parts.stem: The percentage increase in mass of group A was 20%. Which conclusion is best supported?

options.content: No water can enter a seed except through the micropyle.
options.rationale: Group A still gained 20% in mass, so some water entered elsewhere.

options.content: Most of the water enters through the micropyle, but some passes through the testa.
options.rationale: Sealing the micropyle cut the gain from 58% to 20% but did not stop it.

options.content: The micropyle has no part in water uptake.
options.rationale: Sealing it greatly reduced the gain in mass.

options.content: The nail varnish added mass to the seeds.
options.rationale: The varnish was on the seeds before the first weighing, so it does not explain the gain.

parts.label: (c)
parts.stem: Explain why Chipo compared percentage increases rather than the increases in mass.

points.description: The two groups had different starting masses, so percentages allow a fair comparison

parts.explanation: The groups started with different masses ($5.20\ \text{g}$ and $5.00\ \text{g}$), so percentage change compares them fairly.

parts.label: (d)
parts.stem: Suggest why Chipo dried the surfaces of the seeds before the second weighing.

points.description: To remove water on the outside, so that only water absorbed by the seeds is measured

parts.explanation: Water clinging to the outside would add mass that had not been absorbed, so drying makes the measurement accurate.

parts.label: (e)
parts.stem: Name the scar found next to the micropyle on the testa of a bean seed.

rejected.feedback: The plumule is the young shoot inside the seed. The scar is the hilum.

explanation: Group B gained $7.90 - 5.00 = 2.90\ \text{g}$, which is 58% of its starting mass, while group A gained only 20%. Sealing the micropyle greatly reduced water uptake, so most water enters through the micropyle, although some passes through the testa.
workedSolution:
**(a)** Increase $= 7.90 - 5.00 = 2.90\ \text{g}$; $2.90 \div 5.00 \times 100 = 58\%$.

**(b)** A: $(6.24 - 5.20) \div 5.20 \times 100 = 20\%$, less than B but not zero.

**(c)** Different starting masses.

**(d)** Only absorbed water should be weighed.

**(e)** Hilum.

stem:
A biology class collected these fruits and seeds from around their school in Mutare.

- **P**: a round, yellow-brown fruit with soft, sweet flesh around hard seeds
- **Q**: a thin, dry, black fruit with two to four barbed bristles at one end
- **R**: a flat, woody pod that had split into two twisted halves
- **S**: a light, dry fruit with four thin, papery wings

parts.label: (a)
parts.stem: Match each fruit with its method of dispersal.

right.content: Carried on animal fur or clothing

parts.label: (b)
parts.stem: Explain how the seeds of fruit P are carried away from the parent tree.

points.description: Animals (or people) are attracted to and eat the sweet, soft fruit
The hard seeds are spat out or survive digestion and pass out in droppings, away from the tree

parts.explanation: Animals and people eat the sweet flesh; the hard seeds are spat out or swallowed and pass out undamaged in droppings, away from the parent tree.

parts.label: (c)
parts.stem: Give **two** reasons why it is an advantage to a plant for its seeds to be dispersed.

points.description: Less overcrowding / competition (with the parent and each other) for light, water, mineral ions or space
Colonises new areas / better chance of survival of the species

parts.explanation: Dispersed seedlings compete less with the parent and each other for light, water and mineral ions, and the species can colonise new areas.

explanation: P is a fleshy fruit (eaten by animals), Q has barbed bristles (hooks onto fur and clothing), R is an explosive pod (self-dispersal) and S has papery wings (wind). Dispersal reduces competition and lets the species colonise new areas.
workedSolution:
**(a)** P eaten by animals; Q on fur or clothing; R explosive pod; S wind.

**(b)** Sweet flesh is eaten; hard seeds are spat out or pass out in droppings.

**(c)** Less competition / overcrowding; colonising new areas.
hints: Look for flesh, barbs, a split pod and wings.

stem: Explain why seed dispersal is important to flowering plants, and describe, with a named example of each, how fruits or seeds are adapted for dispersal by wind, by animals and by self-dispersal. [8]

points.description: Dispersal reduces overcrowding and competition with the parent and between seedlings (for light, water, mineral ions, space)
Dispersal lets the species colonise new areas / increases its chances of survival
Wind: wings or hairs give a large surface area / air resistance, so the fruit falls slowly and drifts
Named wind example, e.g. Combretum (winged fruit), jacaranda (winged seed) or milkweed (hairy seed)
Animals: hooks or barbs catch on fur or clothing, e.g. blackjack
Animals: fleshy, sweet, coloured fruits are eaten; hard-coated seeds survive digestion and pass out in droppings, e.g. mazhanje, marula
Self-dispersal: pods dry unevenly and split suddenly, flinging the seeds out
Named self-dispersal example, e.g. bean, cowpea or msasa pods

answerSpec.modelAnswer:
Seeds that fall beneath the parent are overcrowded: the seedlings compete with each other and with the parent for light, water, mineral ions and space. Dispersal reduces this competition and lets the species colonise new areas, so more seedlings survive.

Wind-dispersed fruits and seeds are light and have wings or hairs that give a large surface area and air resistance, so they fall slowly and drift. Combretum fruits, for example, have four papery wings.

Some animal-dispersed fruits have hooks or barbs that catch on fur or clothing, such as blackjack. Others, such as mazhanje and marula, are sweet and fleshy; animals eat them, and the hard seeds are spat out or pass through the gut undamaged and are dropped in the dung far from the parent.

In self-dispersal, pods such as those of beans, cowpeas and msasa dry unevenly until they split suddenly and twist, flinging the seeds away from the plant.

explanation: A full answer gives two reasons for dispersal and, for each method, the adaptation, how it works and a named example.
hints: Plan: importance (2 points), then wind, animals (hooks and fleshy fruits) and self-dispersal, each with a feature and an example.

stem: A tree species produces large fruits with hard seeds; the fruits are eaten mainly by elephants. In a part of a park where elephants have been absent for many years, most of the tree's seeds are found lying beneath the parent trees and very few young trees are growing. Which is the **best** explanation?

options.content: Without elephants the seeds are not carried away, so seedlings under the parents are overcrowded and compete with them for light and water
options.rationale: The trees depend on elephants for dispersal; seedlings beneath the parent struggle.

options.content: Without elephants the trees cannot be pollinated, so no seeds form
options.rationale: Seeds are present, so pollination and fertilisation have happened.

options.content: Elephants are needed to supply the seeds with water through their dung
options.rationale: Seeds absorb water from the soil; dung adds some nutrients but is not the reason here.

options.content: The seeds can only germinate after being dispersed by wind
options.rationale: These large, hard seeds in heavy fruits are suited to animal dispersal, not wind.

explanation: The trees rely on elephants to eat their fruits and drop the seeds far away. Without elephants, seeds fall beneath the parents, where the seedlings are overcrowded and must compete with the large parent trees, so few survive.
hints: Seeds have formed, so the problem is not pollination. What role did the elephants play?

stem: Around one Combretum tree, Farai counted 80 seedlings: 12 were within $5\ \text{m}$ of the tree, 28 were between $5\ \text{m}$ and $10\ \text{m}$ away, and 40 were more than $10\ \text{m}$ away. Calculate the percentage of the seedlings that were more than $5\ \text{m}$ from the tree.
explanation: Seedlings more than $5\ \text{m}$ away: $28 + 40 = 68$. Percentage $= 68 \div 80 \times 100 = 85\%$. Most seedlings grew well away from the parent, as expected for wind-dispersed fruits.
hints: Both the 5-10 m group and the more-than-10 m group are more than 5 m away.
